newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians vote "yes" to new constitution - radio.
newsitem.headline: Algerians vote "yes" to new constitution - radio.

text.p: Algerians have voted overwhelmingly for a draft constitution that would ban Islamic political parties, Algeria's state radio reported on Friday.
The radio, basing its report on provisional referendum returns from several regions, said there would be a large "yes" vote.

State media said threats of violence by Moslem militants had not materialised. Official figures showed Algerians had turned out in large numbers to vote in defiance of the threats and calls by main opposition leaders for a boycott.

High "yes" returns were reported in a number of regions, including 95 percent in the western town of Mascra and more than 90 percent in the southeastern region of El Oued and the southwestern province of Saida, said state radio.
The Berber-dominated northeastern town of Tizi-Ouzou was an exception with nearly 63 percent of the voters opposing the draft constitution, the radio added.
The planned constitution, which says Arabic is the sole state language, has angered Berber activists who want official recognition for their language as well.
Algeria's state-run television said Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour would meet journalists in Algiers at about 9.30 a.m (0830 GMT) to issue final voting figures.
Polls closed at 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Thursday but by early evening nearly three-quarters of Algeria's 16.4 million eligible voters had cast ballots, state radio said, quoting the Interior Ministry.

Residents in the garrison town of Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, said the army shelled mountains near the city on Wednesday night, apparently trying to pre-empt any buildup of Moslem guerrillas. Blida is a route for guerrillas seeking to carry out attacks around Algiers.
The draft constitution would ban Moslem militants from gaining power and guerrillas threatened before the referendum that they would kill anyone voting.
Algiers-based diplomats said the government deployed more than 300,000 soldiers and policemen to guard voters across the country, five times the size of France.
Police and paramilitary forces were seen patrolling Algiers streets under drizzling rain. Soldiers in combat gear manned roadblocks on main routes outside the city, witnesses said.
More than 60,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since 1992 when the authorities annulled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
The Armed Islamic Group, or GIA -- most feared of the country's Moslem guerrilla movements -- warned people not to vote on Thursday, threatening to slit the throats of anyone who left home.
A smiling Zeroual, who cast his ballot at a polling station near the presidential palace in Algiers, vowed to respect the voters' decision on his proposed reforms.
"The Algerian people is sovereign. Its will would be respected," Zeroual, a former army general, told reporters after he voted amid tight security.
Diplomats said hopes for change flowered last year but withered when violence continued and people felt the hardship of economic reforms required by overseas creditors.
"A year after the presidential election, political deadlock is still total," secular opposition leader Said Saadi said on Wednesday. "Social poverty is worsening every day."

"Even before the results of the referendum are known, the conclusions on the future of democracy are far from being optimistic," the Algerian Liberte newspaper said in a comment blasting the government for its tight control on the media.
